newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader offers hostage-takers amnesty.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader offers hostage-takers amnesty.

text.p: Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov, battling a wave of abductions in his breakaway region, on Thursday offered an amnesty to hostage takers on condition that they release their victims by August 10.
Kidnappers failing to comply with the deadline face the death penalty or life imprisonment, Chechnya's general prosecutor Khavazh Serbiyev said in a statement.
Earlier on Thursday Interfax news agency reported that a Russian soldier held captive for a month and a half had been freed by security forces, the fifth to be released this week.

Hostage-taking has become a huge problem in the turbulent Caucasus region where Russian troops fought separatist forces for 21 months until last August. Several foreigners, including two Britons, are still missing after being seized by gunmen.
The abductions have hampered Chechnya's efforts to improve its image and to attract desperately needed funds to rebuild its shattered economy.

As Maskhadov stepped up the fight against the hostage-takers Ivan Rybkin, secretary of Russia's Security Council, flew into the Chechen capital Grozny to prepare the ground for a meeting between the Chechen leader and President Boris Yeltsin.
Interfax news agency quoted Rybkin as saying the meeting, sought by both men to help put the delicate peace process back on track, would take place "in the next seven days".

Rybkin played down comments by Russian First Deputy Fuel and Energy Minister Sergei Kiriyenko on Wednesday that Moscow might build a section of oil pipeline around Chechnya because of problems sealing an oil transport deal with Grozny.
"I believe the Baku-Grozny-Novorossiisk route is the most advantageous for all sides," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Rybkin as saying.
But he added one pipeline might not be enough to handle all the oil expected to flow from the oilfields in the Caspian Sea.
